analogy.p: Imagine a sports hall of fixed size in which 6.02 × 10²³ people are spread out far apart. Whether they are toddlers or basketball players makes almost no difference to the amount of hall space needed, because it is the empty space between them that fills the hall. In the same way, one mole of helium, oxygen or carbon dioxide takes up the same 24 dm³ at RTP, although the masses are very different. The analogy breaks down because real people stand still, whereas gas particles move rapidly and randomly, and the volume changes with temperature and pressure while the number of people does not affect the room's size.
analogy.t: A sports hall full of people

bullets: Recall and apply: **equal moles of any gas occupy equal volumes** at the same temperature and pressure.
Recall: **1 mole of any gas = 24 dm³ at RTP (20 °C, 1 atm)**.
Calculate the **volume of a gas** at RTP from its mass and Mr (mass → moles → volume).
Calculate the **mass of a substance** from the volume of a gas (volume → moles → mass).
Calculate **volumes of gaseous reactants and products** using the ratio in a balanced equation.
Use volumes of gases to **deduce the balanced equation**.
The link between all of these is the **mole**.
core.h: What you must know and do
core.p: This spec point is **Higher tier** and **separate chemistry (triple) only**. You must know that **equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume** under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, and that the volume of **one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20 °C and 1 atmosphere) is 24 dm³**. You must then be able to calculate the volume of a gas at RTP from its mass and Mr, calculate masses from gas volumes, work out **reacting volumes of gases** from a balanced equation, and use volumes to **deduce** a balanced equation. These are common 4 to 6 mark calculation questions.

bullets: Gas particles move **randomly and fast**, and collide with the container walls, creating **pressure**.
The particles are far apart, so the **size** of each particle is negligible compared with the space around it.
Same number of particles + same temperature + same pressure = **same volume**.
This is why **mass differs** between gases (He 4 g, O₂ 32 g, CO₂ 44 g per mole) but volume does not.
It only works for **gases**: a mole of a solid or liquid has a volume that depends on the substance.
Increasing the temperature or decreasing the pressure increases the volume of a mole, so **24 dm³ is only true at RTP**.
core.h: Avogadro's law and why it works
core.p: The statement that equal moles of gases occupy the same volume is known as **Avogadro's law**. One mole of any substance contains the same number of particles, **6.02 × 10²³** (the Avogadro constant). In a gas, the particles are **very far apart** compared with their own size, so the volume of the gas depends almost entirely on the **space between the particles**, which is set by the temperature and pressure, and not on the size or mass of the particles themselves. Therefore, a mole of small helium atoms and a mole of large carbon dioxide molecules take up the same volume.

bullets: **1 mole = 24 dm³ = 24 000 cm³** at RTP.
**0.5 mole = 12 dm³**, **2 moles = 48 dm³**, **0.1 mole = 2.4 dm³**.
If the conditions are not RTP the value would be different (the question would have to give it).
The value can be derived from the ideal gas equation (V = nRT ÷ p gives about 24 dm³ at 293 K and 101 kPa), but that is **beyond GCSE**.
Units: **dm³/mol** for molar volume.
Volume is measured in **dm³** (litres) for large amounts and **cm³** for small amounts in the lab.
core.p: The **molar volume** of a gas is the volume occupied by one mole of it. At **room temperature and pressure (RTP)**, defined as **20 °C and 1 atmosphere**, one mole of any gas occupies **24 dm³** (24 000 cm³). The AQA specification expects you to remember this value, and questions normally state the conditions or give them as 'at room temperature and pressure'. It is a **constant** for all gases, so you do not need the identity of the gas to convert between moles and volume.

bullets: **Moles = mass (g) ÷ Mr**, so **mass = moles × Mr**.
**Volume of gas (dm³) = moles × 24**.
**Moles of gas = volume (dm³) ÷ 24**.
If the volume is in cm³: **moles = volume (cm³) ÷ 24 000**.
**1 dm³ = 1000 cm³** (and 1 dm³ = 1 litre).
Combined: **volume (dm³) = (mass ÷ Mr) × 24**.
Check: a mole of any gas at RTP has a **mass in grams equal to Mr** and a **volume of 24 dm³**.
core.p: There are only a few equations, and all are rearrangements of one another. The key is to be able to move between **mass**, **moles** and **volume** in either direction. The relative formula mass **Mr** converts mass to moles, and **24 dm³/mol** converts moles to volume. Always write the **units** at each step, because a mistake with dm³ and cm³ is the most common error. Do not round until the final step.

bullets: Step 1: write the **balanced equation** and identify the ratio between the known substance and the gas.
Step 2: **moles = mass ÷ Mr** for the known substance.
Step 3: **ratio** from the equation gives **moles of gas**.
Step 4: **volume = moles × 24** (dm³); multiply by 1000 for cm³ if asked.
Example: 5.00 g CaCO₃ (Mr 100) → 0.0500 mol; CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ is 1 : 1, so 0.0500 mol CO₂ = 0.0500 × 24 = **1.20 dm³ (1200 cm³)**.
State the answer with the **unit** and to the correct **significant figures**.
core.h: Calculating a gas volume from a mass
core.p: This is the most common question type: you are given a mass of a reactant or product and asked what volume of gas is formed or needed. The method is: **balanced equation** → **moles of the substance you know** → **use the ratio to find moles of the gas** → **multiply by 24**. Pay careful attention to which substance the mass relates to, and to the number in front of the gas in the equation. If the gas is the one you are given, you skip the ratio step.

bullets: **Moles of gas = volume (dm³) ÷ 24**.
Use the **equation ratio** to find the moles of the solid reactant.
**Mass = moles × Mr** (or Ar for an element).
Example: 120 cm³ H₂ = 0.120 dm³; 0.120 ÷ 24 = 0.00500 mol; Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ is 1 : 1, so 0.00500 mol Mg; mass = 0.00500 × 24 = **0.120 g Mg**.
A common check: if the gas volume is small (cm³), the mass will be small (mg to g).
If the volume is given in **cm³**, the shortcut moles = V ÷ 24 000 avoids the conversion.
core.h: Calculating a mass from a gas volume
core.p: The reverse calculation starts with a measured volume of gas and asks for the mass of a reactant or product. The route is the same but reversed: **volume → moles of gas → ratio → moles of the other substance → mass**. This type is common in the **required practical**-style questions where a metal or carbonate reacts with acid and a gas syringe measures the gas. Make sure the volume is converted into dm³ before dividing by 24, or else divide cm³ by 24 000.

bullets: For CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, **50 cm³ CH₄ needs 100 cm³ O₂** and makes **50 cm³ CO₂**.
The **ratio of volumes = ratio of big numbers** in the equation.
Volumes can be in any **consistent** unit (cm³, dm³) because they are only compared with each other.
The shortcut is only valid for **gases at the same T and p**.
Water is normally a **liquid at RTP**, so its volume is ignored unless it is stated as steam.
If a reactant is in **excess**, the leftover volume must be added to the final total of gas.
core.p: When **all substances in a reaction are gases**, the volumes of the gases react in the **same ratio as the moles in the balanced equation**, because equal moles occupy equal volumes. You can therefore skip the mole calculation: just use the equation ratio on the volumes. This only works if all volumes are measured at the **same temperature and pressure**. Substances which are solids or liquids are ignored, because their volume is not related to moles in the same way.

bullets: Example: 25 cm³ N₂ + 75 cm³ H₂ → 50 cm³ NH₃.
Divide by the smallest (25): **1 : 3 : 2**.
Balanced equation: **N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃**.
Check the atoms: 2 N and 6 H on each side.
If you get a ratio like 1 : 1.5 : 1, **multiply by 2** to get whole numbers.
State symbols (g) are needed because the ratio only works for gases.
core.h: Deducing a balanced equation from volumes
core.p: You can use experimental volumes of gases to **work out the balanced equation**. Divide each volume by the **smallest** one, which gives the simplest whole-number ratio of moles, and these are the big numbers in the equation. This is a typical Higher tier question that links reacting volumes to equations. The identity of each substance (formulae) is given, and you only supply the coefficients.

bullets: Look at the **state symbols**: (g) means gas; (s), (l), (aq) are not included in volume calculations.
At RTP, **water is liquid**, so H₂O(l) does not contribute to the gas volume.
The **limiting reactant** decides the maximum volume of gas formed.
If a gas is in excess, the **remaining volume** of it is added to the products.
A **smaller volume** than expected may be due to gas dissolving, leaks or incomplete reaction.
Question wording like **'excess acid'** means the solid is the limiting reactant.
core.h: State symbols, excess and what to count
core.p: Only **gases** are counted in reacting-volume problems. In the equation CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) there is only **one gas**, CO₂, so the volume of gas collected is the volume of CO₂ alone. When an acid or other reactant is in **excess**, the amount of gas depends on the **limiting reactant**, which is the one that is completely used up. Identify it by calculating moles of each reactant and dividing by its coefficient.

bullets: **Gas syringe**: barrel with a plunger that is pushed out as gas collects; read the volume from the scale in **cm³**.
**Upturned measuring cylinder** filled with water; the gas displaces the water and the volume of gas is the volume of water pushed out.
Check for **leaks** at joints and bungs and that the syringe plunger moves freely.
**Hazards**: acid is an irritant (wear **eye protection**); hydrogen is **flammable**; do not stopper a flask without an outlet.
Measure the volume at a **constant temperature**; the gas warms during exothermic reactions and expands.
Compare the measured volume with the **calculated maximum volume** to find the percentage yield.
core.h: Measuring gas volumes in the lab
core.p: Gas volumes can be measured by **collecting gas in a gas syringe** or by displacing water from an **upturned measuring cylinder (or burette)** in a trough of water. The gas syringe is **more accurate** because it reads directly to the nearest 1 cm³ and the gas does not dissolve. When using water displacement, a gas that **dissolves in water** (such as carbon dioxide) gives too small a volume. Experiments should be set up with no leaks, and the bung must be put in **quickly** to avoid losing gas.

bullets: **Gradient = change in volume ÷ change in moles = 24 dm³/mol**.
Directly proportional: **doubling the moles doubles the volume**.
On a volume–time graph, the **plateau** shows the reaction has finished.
A **steeper curve** means a **faster** rate; the same final volume means the **same amount** of limiting reactant.
Read the volume from the **y-axis**, check the **units** (cm³ or dm³).
Use a ruler for **construction lines** to read the value.
core.p: A graph of **volume of gas against amount in moles** is a **straight line through the origin** whose **gradient is the molar volume**, 24 dm³/mol at RTP. A graph of **volume of gas against time** for a reaction produces a curve that starts steeply and **levels off** when the limiting reactant is used up; the final volume is the maximum. You may be asked to read the final volume, convert it to moles and then to the mass of reactant, or to use the **gradient**.

bullets: Always write the **units** of every intermediate value.
The route is **mass ÷ Mr → moles → ratio → moles × 24 → volume**.
For mass questions reverse the route: **volume ÷ 24 → moles → ratio → moles × Mr**.
Use Ar from the Periodic Table: **H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, Mg = 24, Ca = 40**.
Do not round until the **last step**; give 3 significant figures.
If a **diatomic gas** (H₂, O₂, N₂, Cl₂) is involved, its Mr is **twice** its Ar (e.g. O₂ = 32).
core.p: Use the same checklist for every gas volume question: read the **conditions** (RTP?), write the **equation**, identify which substance has the **known** quantity, convert to **moles**, use the **ratio**, convert to the **required quantity**, and then check the answer for **sense** (units, magnitude). Common checks: 24 dm³ of gas is a lot (like a large bucket), so a few grams of reactant normally give **cm³ to a few dm³**. Show the working in full because **marks are given for each step**.

bullets: Link to **rates**: volume of gas against time graphs, and a gas syringe as measuring apparatus.
Link to **acid reactions**: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen; carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Link to **tests for gases**: hydrogen pops with a lit splint; carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.
Link to **titration**: both use moles with solutions and gases; same stoichiometry steps.
Link to **yield**: percentage yield = actual volume ÷ theoretical volume × 100.
Link to the **atmosphere**: knowing the volume of gases at RTP helps with questions on air composition, e.g. 21% oxygen.
core.p: Gas volume calculations extend the **mole** ideas of quantitative chemistry and connect to several other topics. In **rates of reaction**, the volume of gas collected over time is a standard method for following a reaction. In **energy and bonding**, gases such as hydrogen and oxygen are used as fuels. In **chemical changes**, metals and carbonates react with acids to give hydrogen and carbon dioxide. In **atom economy and yield**, the volume of gas can be used to calculate a **percentage yield**. Know these connections for unfamiliar-context questions.

exam: **Recall** questions (1 mark): state that **one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at RTP**; give RTP as **20 °C and 1 atmosphere**.
**Calculate the volume of gas** (3 to 4 marks): moles from mass ÷ Mr, ratio from equation, volume = moles × 24, with correct unit.
**Calculate the mass** from a gas volume (3 to 4 marks): volume ÷ 24 (or cm³ ÷ 24 000), ratio, then moles × Mr.
**Deduce the equation** from volumes: divide by the smallest volume, write whole-number coefficients, check atoms balance.
**Explain** why different gases have the same molar volume: particles are far apart, so volume depends on the number of particles, not their size (Avogadro's law).
Always check whether the volume is in **cm³ or dm³**; examiners often set the trap on purpose.
In a **6-mark** question, link the steps in order: equation, moles of reactant, ratio, moles of gas, volume, and a comment on conditions.
For **graph** questions, state the **gradient** or read the **plateau** and show construction lines.
Commonly asked: **why the volume collected is less than calculated** (gas dissolves, leak, reaction incomplete, gas lost before bung).
Give answers to **3 significant figures** unless told otherwise, and include units (dm³ or cm³).
Command words: **calculate** (show working), **deduce** (use the data to work out), **explain** (because...), **suggest** (apply knowledge to an unfamiliar context).

mistakes.r: 24 dm³ is correct only at room temperature and pressure (20 °C, 1 atm).
mistakes.w: Using 24 for the volume of a mole at any temperature.

mistakes.r: Convert 120 cm³ to 0.120 dm³ first, or use 24 000 cm³ per mole.
mistakes.w: Mixing up cm³ and dm³ (e.g. 120 cm³ ÷ 24).

mistakes.r: Divide mass by Mr to get moles, then multiply by 24.
mistakes.w: Using the mass of the gas without converting to moles.

mistakes.r: Use the big numbers to convert moles of the known substance to moles of the gas.
mistakes.w: Ignoring the ratio in the equation (e.g. 2HCl : 1 H₂).

mistakes.r: Only gases are included, and water is a liquid at RTP.
mistakes.w: Counting water or solids when working out the volume of gas produced.

mistakes.r: Use Mr: O₂ = 32, H₂ = 2, N₂ = 28, Cl₂ = 71.
mistakes.w: Using Ar instead of Mr for a diatomic gas such as O₂ or H₂.

mistakes.r: Equal moles of any gas occupy equal volume; the particles are far apart so their size does not matter.
mistakes.w: Saying a heavier gas takes up more volume.

mistakes.r: The volume-ratio shortcut works only for gases at the same temperature and pressure.
mistakes.w: Using the ratio of volumes for solutions or solids.

mistakes.r: Moles have the unit mol; volume dm³ or cm³.
mistakes.w: Forgetting units or writing dm3 as the unit for moles.

summary: You must know that equal moles of gases occupy equal volumes at the same temperature and pressure, with one mole of any gas occupying 24 dm³ at RTP (20 °C, 1 atm), and use this (Higher tier, triple) to convert between mass, moles and gas volume and to find reacting volumes and equations. It matters because it is a frequent multi-step calculation.

svg.cap: Reacting volumes. Gas volumes at the same temperature and pressure react in the ratio of the balanced equation: methane burns with twice its volume of oxygen to give an equal volume of carbon dioxide (water is a liquid and ignored). Dividing the volumes in the nitrogen/hydrogen/ammonia example by the smallest gives 1 : 3 : 2.

terms.d: The unit for amount of substance; one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) and its mass in grams equals its relative formula mass.
The number of particles in one mole of a substance, 6.02 × 10²³ per mole.
Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
The volume occupied by one mole of a gas; 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.
Room temperature and pressure: 20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula.
The average mass of an atom of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Cubic decimetre, equal to 1000 cm³ or one litre.
The volumes of gases that react or are produced; they are in the same ratio as the moles in the balanced equation at the same temperature and pressure.
An equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, whose big numbers give the ratio of moles.
The reactant that is completely used up first, which determines the amount of product formed.
A reactant present in a larger amount than needed, so some is left unreacted.
Apparatus with a graduated barrel and plunger used to collect and measure the volume of a gas.
Letters (s), (l), (g), (aq) in an equation showing the physical state of each substance.
A molecule made of two atoms, e.g. H₂, N₂, O₂, Cl₂.
The maximum mass or volume of product that could be made from the given amount of reactant, from the equation.

worked.q: Calcium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced at RTP from 5.00 g of calcium carbonate. Ar: Ca 40, C 12, O 16. (4 marks)
steps: Ratio CaCO₃ : CO₂ = 1 : 1, so moles CO₂ = 0.0500 mol.

worked.q: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. A student collects 120 cm³ of hydrogen at RTP. Calculate the mass of magnesium that reacted. Ar Mg = 24. (4 marks)
steps: Ratio Mg : H₂ = 1 : 1, so moles Mg = 0.00500 mol.

worked.q: 25 cm³ of nitrogen reacts with 75 cm³ of hydrogen to make 50 cm³ of ammonia, all measured at the same temperature and pressure. Deduce the balanced equation, and state the volume of hydrogen needed to make 200 cm³ of ammonia. (3 marks)
steps: Divide each volume by the smallest (25): N₂ : H₂ : NH₃ = 1 : 3 : 2.
Equation: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ (atoms: 2 N and 6 H on each side).
